title: Gauss chart for ordered blocks as a scheme isomorphism
statement:
Let $F$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $s\geq0$, and let $E=\bigoplus_{i=1}^s E_i$ be a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space with each $E_i$ nonzero. Groups and general linear groups have the meanings of [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sc-general-linear-group]; in dimension zero take $\operatorname{GL}(0)=1$. Define $L,U\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(E)$ on each commutative $F$-algebra to be the block lower and block upper unitriangular matrices: each diagonal block is the identity and every block strictly above, respectively strictly below, the diagonal is zero. Let $D=\prod_{i=1}^s\operatorname{GL}(E_i)$ embedded by block diagonal matrices. For $1\leq j\leq s$, let $\Delta_j(g)$ be the determinant of the block of $g$ on $\bigoplus_{i\leq j}E_i$, using arbitrary fixed bases [def-weil-pbc-matrix-determinant]. Then multiplication is an isomorphism of $F$-schemes, with fibre products as in [def-pc-fibre-product],
$$L\times_F D\times_F U\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal V,\qquad (l,d,u)\mapsto ldu,$$
where $\mathcal V\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(E)$ is the principal open $\prod_j\Delta_j\ne0$ [def-weil-open-immersion]. Equivalently its $A$-points are exactly those $g$ for which every $\Delta_j(g)$ is a unit in $A$. The inverse gives unique block Gauss factors, functorially over every commutative $F$-algebra $A$. The isomorphism and its inverse are equivariant for conjugation by every block diagonal matrix. For $s=0$ all schemes are $1$ and the product of minors is $1$.

source.place: Section 23h, equation (153), Theorem 23.72 and Notes, printed pp.510-511. Agent-stated supporting lemma: General matrix lemma for the immersion step, proved by iterating the two-block Schur-complement identity; it imposes no root-theoretic or reductivity hypothesis.

proof.text: For $s=0$ the empty matrix and all three factors represent the terminal $F$-scheme, and the empty determinant product is $1$. Assume $s>0$ and choose bases in the blocks. The strictly lower entries are independent coordinates: $I+N$ is invertible with inverse $\sum_{k=0}^{s-1}(-N)^k$, since a nonzero term of $N^s$ would require $s+1$ strictly ordered block indices. Hence $L$ is represented by the polynomial algebra on these coordinates; the same construction with reversed inequalities gives $U$. The polynomial universal property and the affine-spectrum correspondence give these representing schemes, with their stated inclusions into $\operatorname{GL}(E)$. Each factor of $D$ has the localized determinant presentation of the general-linear-group definition. By the affine fibre-product statement, $L\times_FD\times_FU$ (and likewise $D\times_F\mathcal V$, $D\times_FL\times_FD\times_FU$) is affine with ring the tensor product of the coordinate rings; by the tensor-product universal property its $A$-points are the triples of $A$-points, and this ring is the polynomial algebra on all off-diagonal and diagonal-block entries localized at the diagonal-block determinants, so it represents the independent choices of the entries and inverse determinants. Put $H=\Gamma(\operatorname{GL}(E),\mathcal O)$ and $f=\prod_j\Delta_j$. The principal open $\mathcal V$ is affine with ring $H_f$ by the affine-open localization statement (Stacks 01I3, schemes-lemma-standard-open-affine). The localization universal property identifies its $A$-points with matrices in $\operatorname{GL}(E)(A)$ for which $f$ is a unit. In a commutative ring this is equivalent to each $\Delta_j$ being a unit: if $f v=1$, then $v\prod_{k\ne j}\Delta_k$ is an inverse of $\Delta_j$.

source.place: Agent-written general matrix argument supporting §23h, Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510–511 (Milne omits the details). Coordinate constructions; Stacks 01I3 and 00CP supply the open and its points.

proof.text: For any commutative $F$-algebra $A$ and any $(l,d,u)$, restricting $ldu$ to the first $j$ blocks gives $l_{\le j}d_{\le j}u_{\le j}$: a term in the product has its intermediate index at most the row block for $l$ and at most the column block for $u$. Applying the two-block determinant identity repeatedly with pivot $I$ shows that a lower or upper unitriangular matrix has determinant $1$ (its Schur complement is the remaining unitriangular block). Thus determinant multiplicativity gives $\Delta_j(ldu)=\prod_{i\le j}\det(d_i)$, a unit; for block diagonal matrices the same product formula follows recursively from the Schur identity with zero off-diagonal blocks. Each $\det(d_i)$ is a unit because applying multiplicativity to $d_i d_i^{-1}=I$ gives an inverse. Matrix multiplication is polynomial in the entries. In the coordinate ring of $L\times D\times U$ the formula just proved makes $f(ldu)$ a unit. Polynomial evaluation, the localization universal property and the affine-spectrum correspondence therefore give the multiplication morphism $m:L\times D\times U\to\mathcal V$.

source.place: Agent-written general matrix argument supporting §23h, Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510–511 (Milne omits the details). The multiplication morphism and the leading-minor image calculation.

proof.text:
Prove by induction on $s$, uniformly for all commutative $F$-algebras $A$, that every $g\in\mathcal V(A)$ admits factors. The $s=0$ case is step 1; for $s=1$ use $(I,g,I)$. For $s\ge2$ write $g=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}P&Q\\ T&W\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, splitting off $E_1$. Since $\det P=\Delta_1(g)$ is a unit, the adjugate identity gives $P^{-1}=(\det P)^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(P)$. Set $S=W-TP^{-1}Q$. Apply the Schur determinant identity to the first $k+1$ blocks of $g$ to get $\Delta_{k+1}(g)=\det P\,\Delta_k(S)$ for $1\le k\le s-1$. Consequently every $\Delta_k(S)$ is a unit. The full one makes $S$ invertible by the adjugate identity, so the induction hypothesis applies to $S$ on $E_2\oplus\cdots\oplus E_s$. Write $S=l'd'u'$. If $L_0=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I&0\\ TP^{-1}&I\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $U_0=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I&P^{-1}Q\\0&I\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, the Schur factorization yields
$$g=\bigl(L_0\operatorname{diag}(I,l')\bigr)\operatorname{diag}(P,d')\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(I,u')U_0\bigr).$$
These three factors have exactly the required lower-unitriangular, invertible block-diagonal and upper-unitriangular forms. This establishes existence without a field or reducedness assumption on $A$.

source.place: Agent-written general matrix argument supporting §23h, Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510–511 (Milne omits the details). Induction using the two-block Schur identities, including the explicit assembled factors.

proof.text: For uniqueness use the same induction. In any factorization write $l=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I&0\\ x&l'\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, $d=\operatorname{diag}(p,d')$ and $u=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I&y\\0&u'\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Block multiplication gives $P=p$, $Q=py$, $T=xp$, $W=xpy+l'd'u'$. Hence $p=P$, $y=P^{-1}Q$, $x=TP^{-1}$, and $l'd'u'=W-TP^{-1}Q=S$. The factors of $S$ are unique by induction, which fixes all three original factors. The base cases $s=0,1$ have no off-diagonal choices. Every algebra homomorphism carries an inverse to an inverse and preserves sums and products, so applying it to a factorization gives the unique factorization of the image matrix. This proves functoriality over all commutative $F$-algebras, including the zero algebra.

source.place: Agent-written general matrix argument supporting §23h, Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510–511 (Milne omits the details). Uniqueness by comparing the four blocks, and naturality by uniqueness.

proof.text: Apply step 3 to the universal matrix over $R=\Gamma(\mathcal V,\mathcal O)=H_f$. It gives actual matrices $l_R,d_R,u_R$ over $R$, with invertible diagonal blocks. The representing coordinate descriptions of step 1 turn them into an $F$-morphism $v:\mathcal V\to L\times D\times U$: the off-diagonal coordinate functions are their entries, the diagonal coordinates are those of $d_R$, and each inverted determinant maps to its inverse in $R$. Existence and uniqueness of these algebra maps use polynomial evaluation and localization. Thus no assertion about field-valued points is used to construct $v$. The identity $l_Rd_Ru_R=g_R$ shows $m\circ v=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal V}$ on coordinate generators and hence as scheme morphisms. Conversely apply uniqueness of step 4 in $B=\Gamma(L\times D\times U,\mathcal O)$ to its universal triple: the factors obtained by $v$ from its product must be that triple. Therefore $v\circ m$ is the identity on each entry and inverse determinant, hence on the entire localized polynomial coordinate ring. The affine-spectrum correspondence proves $m$ and $v$ are inverse isomorphisms. The constructions over $R$ agree with the pointwise inverse over every $A$ by step 4.

source.place: Agent-written general matrix argument supporting §23h, Theorem 23.72, printed pp.510–511 (Milne omits the details). Passage from the all-algebras calculation to mutually inverse scheme morphisms using their universal coordinate rings.

proof.text: Let $h=\operatorname{diag}(h_i)\in D(A)$. Conjugation sends block $(i,j)$ of a matrix to $h_i g_{ij}h_j^{-1}$, preserving all zero and identity blocks and preserving invertibility of diagonal blocks. On the first $j$ blocks it conjugates the leading matrix by $\operatorname{diag}(h_1,\ldots,h_j)$; determinant multiplicativity makes $\Delta_j(hgh^{-1})=\Delta_j(g)$, so it preserves $\mathcal V$. Associativity gives $(hlh^{-1})(hdh^{-1})(huh^{-1})=h(ldu)h^{-1}$, proving equivariance of multiplication. Uniqueness in step 4 then gives equivariance of the inverse. These equalities hold also with $A$ the coordinate ring of $D\times\mathcal V$ or $D\times L\times D\times U$; by the affine-spectrum correspondence they are equalities of action morphisms, so equivariance holds as schemes and after every base change. The empty-block case was settled in step 1.

theorem relative_block_gauss_chart (hr : ∀ i : Fin s, 0 < r i) :
    (∀ t : Fin 3, IsClosedImmersion (factorι A r t).left) ∧
    IsOpenImmersion (cellι A r).left ∧
    Set.range (cellι A r).left =
      (PrimeSpectrum.basicOpen (minors A r) : Set (PrimeSpectrum (Coordinates A r))) ∧
    (∃ d : factor A r 1 ≅ diagonalProduct A r,
      ∀ (B : Type u) [CommRing B] [Algebra A B]
        (x : (Spec (.of B)).asOver (Spec (.of A)) ⟶ factor A r 1),
        (factorPoint A r B 1 x).val = diagonalPoint A r B (x ≫ d.hom)) ∧
    (∀ (B : Type u) [CommRing B] [Algebra A B]
      (g : Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup (Index.{u} r) B),
      (∃ y : (Spec (.of B)).asOver (Spec (.of A)) ⟶ cell A r,
        cellPoint A r B y = g) ↔ ∀ j : Fin s, IsUnit (leadingMinor r g.val j)) ∧
    (∃ e : factors A r ≅ cell A r, IsMultiplication A r e ∧
      (∀ (B : Type u) [CommRing B] [Algebra A B]
        (y : (Spec (.of B)).asOver (Spec (.of A)) ⟶ cell A r),
        ∃! x : (Spec (.of B)).asOver (Spec (.of A)) ⟶ factors A r,
          productPoint A r B x 0 * productPoint A r B x 1 * productPoint A r B x 2 =
            cellPoint A r B y) ∧
      (∀ (B C : Type u) [CommRing B] [CommRing C] [Algebra A B] [Algebra A C]
        (ψ : B →ₐ[A] C) (y : (Spec (.of B)).asOver (Spec (.of A)) ⟶ cell A r)
        (t : Fin 3),
        inverseFactor A r e C
            ((Spec.map (CommRingCat.ofHom ψ.toRingHom)).asOver (Spec (.of A)) ≫ y) t =
          Matrix.GeneralLinearGroup.map ψ.toRingHom (inverseFactor A r e B y t)) ∧
      (∀ (A' : Type u) [CommRing A'] (e' : factors A' r ≅ cell A' r),
        IsMultiplication A' r e' →
        ∀ (B : Type u) [CommRing B] [Algebra A B] [Algebra A' B]
          (y : (Spec (.of B)).asOver (Spec (.of A)) ⟶ cell A r)
          (z : (Spec (.of B)).asOver (Spec (.of A')) ⟶ cell A' r),
          cellPoint A r B y = cellPoint A' r B z →
          ∀ t : Fin 3, inverseFactor A r e B y t = inverseFactor A' r e' B z t) ∧
      (∀ (B : Type u) [CommRing B] [Algebra A B]
        (h : (Spec (.of B)).asOver (Spec (.of A)) ⟶ factor A r 1)
        (y z : (Spec (.of B)).asOver (Spec (.of A)) ⟶ cell A r),
        cellPoint A r B z = factorPoint A r B 1 h * cellPoint A r B y *
            (factorPoint A r B 1 h)⁻¹ →
        ∀ t : Fin 3, inverseFactor A r e B z t =
          factorPoint A r B 1 h * inverseFactor A r e B y t *
            (factorPoint A r B 1 h)⁻¹)) ∧
    (s = 0 → minors A r = 1 ∧
      (∀ t : Fin 3, Nonempty (factor A r t ≅ Over.mk (𝟙 (Spec (.of A))))) ∧
